paragraphs.source_en: In 1987, on what was later to be called Black Monday, I called my broker at the end of a very busy day. Remember that this was when we all still had stockbrokers. When we were in the dark ages before cell phones, personal computers, the internet and online trading.

paragraphs.source_en: As any educated investor does, I knew that the market was volatile. I knew that on its relentless march upwards there could and would be sharp drops, corrections and bear markets. I knew that the best course was to hold firm and not panic. But this? This was a whole ‘nother frame of reference.

paragraphs.source_en: I just wasn’t tough enough. That day when I sold it was, if not the absolute bottom, close enough to it as not to matter. Then, of course and as always, the market again began its inevitable climb. The market always goes up.

paragraphs.source_en: It took a year or so for me to regain my nerve and get back in. By then it had passed its pre-Black Monday high. I had managed to lock in my losses and pay a premium for a seat back at the table. It was expensive. It was stupid. It was an embarrassing failure of nerve. I just wasn’t tough enough.

units.source_en: It took a year or so for me to regain my nerve and get back in.
By then it had passed its pre-Black Monday high.
I had managed to lock in my losses and pay a premium for a seat back at the table.
It was expensive.
It was stupid.
It was an embarrassing failure of nerve.
I just wasn’t tough enough.

paragraphs.source_en: But I am now. My mistake of ’87 taught me exactly how to weather all the future storms that came rolling in, including the Class 5 financial hurricane of 2008. It taught me to be tough and ultimately it made me far more money than the admittedly expensive education cost.
